opus-5.5.text:
I think Operator is interesting precisely because, for a long time, people meant very different things when they said "agent."

If you come from a reinforcement learning background, like I do, an agent is something very classical. It lives in an environment, observes a state, takes an action, gets a reward, and over many interactions learns a policy. That's the Atari agent, the Go agent, the robot agent. The key ideas are decision-making, interaction, and learning from feedback.

Then large language models came along, and "agent" started to mean something else. It meant a language model that can call tools, write some code, search the web, maybe plan a few steps in natural language. That notion is very general and very knowledgeable, but often not that grounded. It reasons in text, while the actual interaction with the world is quite thin, and a lot of it is hand-engineered prompting and workflows rather than learned behavior.

What Operator does, in my view, is put these two pictures into one system. On one side, it has the general knowledge and reasoning ability of a large foundation model. It understands what you want when you say "book me a table" or "fill out this form." On the other side, it really acts in an environment in the RL sense. It looks at the screen, a raw visual observation, and it outputs actions like clicking, typing, and scrolling, step by step over a long horizon. The browser, or the computer, becomes the environment. That's a very general environment, because almost everything humans do digitally goes through that interface.

And importantly, getting this to work reliably isn't just about prompting. You need training, and especially reinforcement learning, to make the model robust when it actually interacts: recovering from mistakes, handling pop-ups, deciding when to ask the user for confirmation. That's where the RL view of an agent really comes back.

So I'd summarize it this way: the LLM gives you the "brain," the prior knowledge and reasoning, and the RL view gives you the "body," acting, getting feedback, and improving through interaction. Operator is one of the first products where these two understandings of an agent come together in something ordinary users can actually touch. It's still early, slow, and makes mistakes, but directionally I think this convergence is what the next few years of agent research will be about.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Operator is actually a very interesting case, because people have been using the word "agent" to mean quite different things, and Operator kind of forces those meanings to meet.

If you look at the academic side, especially people coming from reinforcement learning like myself, an agent has always been something very concrete: an entity that perceives an environment, takes actions, gets feedback, and improves over time. It's a loop. The emphasis is on decision-making and interaction with the environment, not on language per se.

Then after ChatGPT, a second understanding came out of the LLM community. There, an "agent" mostly meant a language model wrapped with tools, prompts, and some planning scaffolding—AutoGPT, these kinds of things. It was really about reasoning in text and calling APIs. The environment was still fairly abstract.

Operator is where these two converge. The model is literally looking at a screen, moving a cursor, clicking buttons, filling in forms. That is a real environment with real states and consequences, which is exactly what the RL people meant. But the brain driving it is a large multimodal model with strong language and visual understanding, which is what the LLM people meant. So you have perception, you have action, you have a feedback loop, and underneath it all you have a foundation model doing the reasoning.

What I find most important is the training signal. Browsing and operating a computer give you an environment where you can actually define whether a task succeeded—did the ticket get booked, did the form get submitted. Once you have that, you can do reinforcement learning on top of the pretrained model, and that is where the two paradigms truly merge rather than just sit side by side. OpenAI's o1 line showed that RL on reasoning works; Operator extends that same idea into interacting with the external world.

Of course it is still early. The reliability isn't there yet, the action space is very long-horizon, and errors compound. But conceptually, I think Operator is a signal that the industry is converging on one definition of an agent: a model that can perceive, act, and learn from the outcome in a real environment. That's the version of the word I've always believed in, so I'm quite happy to see it.

astra-6.text:
I think Operator brings together two ways people use the word “agent.” One is an AI that understands a goal, makes a plan, and decides what to do next. The other is a system that can actually act—click buttons, enter information, and interact with software. The interesting part is connecting those capabilities in a loop: observe, decide, act, and then check what happened.

Imagine asking it to book a trip. Understanding the request is only the beginning. It has to navigate an interface, compare options, handle unexpected results, and recognize when it needs your input. That connects reasoning with execution.

So I see Operator as a concrete meeting point for these understandings. It also makes the challenge clearer: an agent needs more than a good plan. It needs to act reliably, recover from mistakes, and know when to hand control back to the user.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Operator brings together two ways of thinking about an AI agent. One starts with language models: you give the model a goal, and it reasons about what to do and uses tools. The other starts with an agent interacting with an environment: it observes, takes an action, sees what changed, and decides what to do next.

With Operator, those ideas meet at the computer interface. The model needs to understand your request, but it also needs to look at the screen, click, type, and respond to what happens. Producing a good plan is only part of the task; it has to carry that plan through an environment that may behave differently than expected.

So, to me, the interesting connection is between reasoning and action. The language model provides a way to interpret goals, while the interaction loop grounds those goals in something the agent can actually do.
